newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Life tough on Russian peninsula but hope emerges.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Life tough on Russian peninsula but hope emerges.

text.p: The people of Kamchatka are surrounded by volcanoes, live in constant fear of earthquakes and spend half the year battling an icy winter.
Life has never been easy on the remote peninsula, about as far east as you can go from Moscow without leaving Russia, but for some it has become unbearable.
Many of Kamchatka's residents were attracted from other regions only by the unusually high wages the region offered in Soviet days, hoping a short stay would set them up for life.
But that dream died when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991. Savings lost their value almost overnight, prices soared and many people doubt now that they will ever be able to leave.
Big rises in energy prices and transport tariffs have hit local firms badly. As if that were not enough, tough new taxes have left them reeling.
Life for many has become a struggle just to survive. A few, including a doctor and a naval officer, have simply given up and committed suicide.

"Things are getting worse and worse and worse, harder and harder and harder," Eduard Belozertsev, an opposition communist member of Kamchatka's parliament, said in his office in the regional capital Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky.
"We have got to make life better."
GLIMMERS OF HOPE

Glimmers of hope are finally starting to emerge through the gloom. Local businessmen say economic reforms which took a long time to travel the 7,000 km (4,500 miles) from Moscow are now having an effect.
They see signs that the industrial decline which hit Kamchatka and other regions after the Soviet Union's collapse has finally bottomed out.
The regional authorities have stepped up efforts to attract investment to tap the peninsula's natural resources to end years of dependence on fuel shipped in from other parts of Russia.
Even leaders of the region's main lifeline, the fishing industry which has been decimated and demoralised in the last few years, say Kamchatka has a future.

"Because of the high fuel costs and taxes, all that most people can do is make ends meet," said Vladimir Potapenko, head of the Kamchatrybprom fish company and a baron of the Soviet fishing industry before his firm was split into small holdings.
"But I think the period of decline in the industry has finished and we are already on the way up."
TURNING NATURAL ADVERSITY TO ADVANTAGE

Kamchatka is known as the land of "ice and fire" because of its 29 active and more than 200 extinct volcanoes, many of which are still covered in snow this summer. It is also on a ring of high seismic activity and small earthquakes are common.
The aim now is to turn natural adversity to advantage. Local leaders say the hostile terrain includes vast natural resources which could give Kamchatka its own sources of energy.

From natural gas to thermal springs and hot geysers, potential energy sources abound and could be exploited with the help of foreign investment. That would reduce energy costs and help local business and industry.

"If Kamchatka had its own energy, production costs would be much less," said Dmitry Povsner, chairman of the Kamchatsky Commercial Agroprom Bank. "What we must do is make use of what is unique about Kamchatka."
ATTEMPTS TO DEVELOP TOURISM

That includes luring tourists to Kamchatka, considered one of the most inhospitable parts of Russia in tsarist times and closed to foreigners in the Soviet era because of the atomic submarine base in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky's natural harbour.
Kamchatka's beauty is spectacular -- brooding snow-capped volcanoes, a spectacular coastline, clean fast-flowing rivers, lush green valleys, geysers and natural springs.
Snow-covered mountains could house ski resorts, the springs could de developed into health resorts and the region could be a paradise for hikers, climbers, anglers and hunters.

But the problems are also manifold. Much of Kamchatka can be reached only by helicopter or small plane, there are few hotels or facilities and most of the few foreign tourists pay through the nose for "extreme tourism" such as climbing.
Creating decent tourism facitilies would require a lot of time and money, but efforts have begun.

A ski resort near Petrovpavlovsk-Kamchatsky is to be overhauled to bring it up to international standards and new nature reserves are being created to protect the wildlife and beauty. Foreign investment is being sought for building a five-star hotel in the regional capital.
ORDINARY PEOPLE STRUGGLE BUT VOTE FOR REFORMS

The grand plans have little direct impact on most of the almost 300,000 people in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, a city dominated by dirty, squat apartment blocks built in Soviet times which stretch up steep hills from crane-lined docks.
Life remains hard for the elderly and infirm who are receiving free fish this summer to help them get by.
Reforms mean nothing for the doctor who recently killed himself after not being paid for months, or the naval officer who committed suicide last year.

People complain constantly that high taxes make business unprofitable while acknowledging that few pay them. They moan about the high prices which cancel out what are by Russian standards high salaries. Some have not been paid for months.
There is hardly a new building in sight apart from a couple of spanking new banks. Many buildings are in decay.
Yet Kamchatka favoured President Boris Yeltsin, the man who oversaw the economic reforms, over his communist opponent Gennady Zyuganov in last year's presidential election.
It elected Mikhail Zadornov, a liberal, as its representative to Russia's lower house of parliament in 1995 and re-elected Governor Vladimir Biryukov, regarded here as a reformer, last December.

"This shows the mood of the people. They do not want to go backwards," said Iskander Khakimov, editor of the local newspaper Vesti. "We have to get through this difficult period but then, I think, the prospects are good."
